1:
To whom the altars were built they agree; what the number meant they do not. Wesley says the seven altars were built to the true God, since otherwise Balaam would not have urged them to God as an argument for granting the request, and that Balak, though averse from God, would be easily overruled by a prophet who doubtless told him it was vain to address any other than the God of Israel. Henry allows as much, that they seem to have offered to the God of heaven and not to their local deities, but will not let the form pass: the multiplying of altars was degeneracy from the religion of their ancestors and apostasy to idolatry, for those that multiplied altars multiplied gods. Ellicott makes the point from usage, that the patriarchs and their pious descendants never erected more than one altar in one place, so that a plurality of altars was the badge of idolatry; and cites Hengstenberg for instances of the ancients using sacrifice and conjuration to avert calamity, the number seven being significant among Greeks and Romans as well as Israelites.

Where the sevens came from Calvin traces to a corruption of something real. God had indicated something of perfection in the number, by consecrating the seventh day to himself and in the seven lamps; but afterwards many strange superstitions were invented, and under that pretext Satan cunningly deluded wretched men by persuading them that secret virtues were contained in the number seven. The same frivolous subtlety prevailed among profane writers, who sought confirmation of the error throughout nature, alleging the seven planets, as many Pleiades, and the stars of the Wain. From this he judges Balaam's method: the degenerate prophet had never been wont to prophesy from pure revelations, the art of divination in which he boasted having some affinity to magical exorcisms and being infected with many errors, so that being endowed only with a special gift he borrowed devices which savoured of nothing but the illusions of the devil.

What Balaam looked like while doing it divides his two describers. Henry sees only imperiousness and greed: he was proud to have the command of a king and to give law to princes, covering his malice with a show of devotion, though his sacrifice was an abomination, brought with a wicked mind, since he aimed not to honour God with the sacrifices of righteousness but to enrich himself with the wages of unrighteousness; and Balak was as obsequious as Balaam was imperious. Calvin sees an imitation nearly indistinguishable from the real thing: in seeking retirement he imitates the true servants of God, since God has almost always appeared to his servants when separated from the company of men, and you would say he was another Moses when he exhorts the king to persevering prayer that he may be more earnest in supplication.

Who sacrificed and where Balaam went are the smaller questions. Ellicott thinks it more probable that Balak, as a king, performed priestly functions than that Balaam did so alone; Gill infers from the standing by that the sacrifices were burnt offerings and that one may have been peculiarly Balak's, though he was concerned in them all; Keil marks only that this followed the sacrifice. Clarke explains why sacrifice came first, that blessing and cursing in this way were considered religious rites and must always be preceded by sacrifice, as with Isaac before he blessed Jacob and Esau. Wesley reads the posture as significant: Balak was to stand as in God's presence, offering himself as well as his sacrifices, while Balaam went to some solitary place where he might prevail with God to appear. On that place the renderings collide: Ellicott says it is rather a bare or barren height, since the heathen augurs chose elevated places with an extensive prospect, especially barren summits, while Wesley says the word properly signifies the plain.
4:
That God met Balaam at all is the difficulty, and they answer by denying what the meeting might seem to grant. Gill lists the negatives: not in a kind manner, not out of respect to his offerings, not to indulge him with spiritual communion. Calvin calls it wonderful that God should have anything in common with the pollutions of Balaam, since there is no communion between light and darkness; the meeting was no proof of favour, but as he knows how to apply corrupt instruments, so by this false prophet's mouth he promulgated to heathen nations the covenant made with Abraham. Balaam meanwhile boasts of his altars as though he had propitiated God, which Calvin makes the posture of hypocrites, who trust they deserve well of God when they do but provoke his anger. Keil says as much in a phrase, that Balaam thought it necessary, as a true soothsayer, to call God's attention to the altars, whereas God answered not by a natural sign of doubtful meaning but by a distinct and unmistakeable word.

How the word came into his mouth Gill defines carefully: not grace into his heart nor the fear of God within him, but a suggestion of what to say, impressed so strongly that he was obliged to deliver it. Ellicott quotes Bishop Wordsworth: God, who had opened the mouth of the ass contrary to her nature, now opens Balaam's mouth contrary to his own will. Calvin uses the case to mark off the true prophets: God does supply his servants with what they speak, yet the holy prophets were organs of the Spirit in such a way that they gave forth from the heart the treasures God had deposited with them, as Jeremiah did eat the words of God and Ezekiel the roll; we must not conceive an inspiration such as the heathen supposed carried their diviners into ecstasy.

What a parable is here they explain four ways. Gill says the word is used because prophecies are often figurative and enigmatical, the Targums calling it the parable of his prophecy. Wesley calls it an oracular speech, named for the weightiness of the matter and the liveliness of the expressions. Calvin says it signifies all weighty sayings in exalted language, so that Balaam spoke eloquently and in no ordinary strain. Clarke goes furthest: the oracles are in hemistich metre in the original, highly dignified, and may be considered immediate poetic productions of the Spirit of God. Keil supplies the geography, that Aram and the mountains of the East mean Mesopotamia, called in Genesis the land of the sons of the East.

What the disclaimer concedes they take alike. Keil says Balak imagined, like all the heathen, that a magician could dispense blessings and curses at will and constrain his God to serve it; the seer opposes the delusion, since the God of Israel does not curse his people and therefore his servant cannot. Clarke says it was granted on all hands that incantations avail only if God ratifies them. Gill says it was simply impossible, though Balaam had a good will to it, to get Balak's money and honour. Calvin presses hardest: Balaam renounces the very power Balak ascribed to him, since Balak had said he knew that whom Balaam cursed was cursed, as if the power of God were transferred to him, which was nothing else than to depose God from his supremacy. He cautions besides that God does not always restrain the wicked from speaking against his truth, since they often prate at random, but that Balaam was compelled to play a different part and confesses his tongue was tied. Gill adds that where the text has God and the Lord the Targums put the Word of the Lord, whom he takes for the Son of God, so far from cursing his people that he was made a curse for them.
9:
What Balaam could see from that height Calvin turns into an argument for inspiration. Although he beheld the people only from afar, they portended to him something great and formidable; a closer view generally intimidates men, and a body of twenty thousand dazzles the sight as if five times as great, whereas distance shows a thing more truly. Balaam therefore declares, in the spirit of prophecy, that he sees far more in the people of God than his distance would allow, since with ordinary vision he would have beheld them only as dwarfs. Gill and Clarke keep to the topography: Gill that he stood on a rock overlooking Israel in the plains below, Clarke that it was from the high places of Baal, chosen that he might the better see the whole camp.

What dwelling alone means they take four ways that reinforce each other. Clarke says they shall ever be preserved a distinct nation, and calls the prophecy literally fulfilled; Wesley, that they are a distinct kind, God's peculiar people. Ellicott says that in the separate encampment Balaam discerned a type of Israel's essential separation from the surrounding nations, and that when Israel adopted heathen ways it lost its external independence; he quotes Hengstenberg for the long view, that while the Egyptian, Assyrian and Babylonian empires have utterly perished, Israel flourishes anew in the Church. Calvin makes it independence rather than isolation: the people dwell content with their own condition, neither desiring the wealth of others nor seeking their aid; and he meets the objection himself, that Israel's later recourse to Egypt and Assyria is not repugnant to the prophecy, since the question is not the virtue of the people but the blessing of God.

The dust of Jacob they refer to the same promise. Ellicott points back to the word to Abraham, that his seed should be as the dust of the earth, and explains the fourth part from the four encampments. Calvin says it is plain that what Balaam spoke was suggested by God, since he cites the words of God's solemn promise, and adds that although the multitude was afterwards reduced by the people's sin, the word was not vain, since that little body at length expanded to fill the whole world. Gill guards the figure: they are called dust not from their original but from their numbers.

What the closing wish means is the sharpest division here. Clarke rejects the received reading: it has been generally supposed that Balaam prays for a happy death, such as true Christians die, but he is satisfied this is not the meaning, since the death of the righteous then meant being gathered to one's fathers in a good old age, and the second clause is better rendered let my posterity be like his; he supposes Balaam had a presentiment of a premature death and lodges the petition against it. Wesley shifts the referent, taking the righteous of this righteous and holy people, so that the wish is to share Israel's happiness. Calvin keeps the common sense but sharpens the mood: the aspiration is more emphatic than a simple affirmation, Balaam wishing to share their last end while confessing himself unworthy to be reckoned among them. On Balak's reproach Gill says nothing had been done to answer his purpose; Ellicott renders the emphatic Hebrew, that Balaam had blessed to bless; Calvin says the proud man reproaches the prophet as though he had purchased the right of prophecy and the authority to make him speak what he chose, and marks how the reprobate seek God by crooked paths; Henry says a confession of God's overruling power is extorted from a wicked prophet to the confusion of a wicked prince, the curse being turned into a blessing a second time, larger and stronger than the first. Keil records only the answer, that Balaam must speak what the Lord put in his mouth.
13:
Why Balak moved his prophet they explain three ways. Clarke and Wesley take it as a calculation about nerve: Balak thought the sight of so immense a camp had intimidated Balaam, gathering as much from his words about the dust of Jacob, or feared it had raised his fancy to admire the multitude. Henry doubles the alternative and adds the strategy: Balak fancied Balaam either so enamoured with the camp's beauty that he would not curse it or so affrighted with its terror that he durst not, and brought him where he might see only a part, which would appear more despicable, hoping to obtain leave to curse that part and by degrees gain ground, intending to attack the very quarter Balaam then had in his eye. Calvin explains it by the art rather than the man: superstitious persons, having nothing certain, are carried from one speculation to another, and especially imagine some magical power in the sight, as if the eyes contributed to the efficacy of their incantations, which he says was a commonly received opinion, that the gaze of the enchanter had much effect upon his art; Balak therefore removes his sorcerer that he might the better exercise his divinations.

What seeing part of them means Ellicott makes turn on an earlier question. If the received rendering is correct it confirms the interpretation by which Balaam saw the whole host from the first station; but the words may be rendered instead that he sees here only the utmost part and does not see them all. On the first reading, which restricts the earlier view to the host's extremity, a full view would show Balaam the ground of Balak's alarm and induce more strenuous efforts; on the second, which gives him the whole camp at once, the sight of so vast a mass had so overpowered him that he could not utter the curses he wished, and a partial view would not. He leaves the alternative standing. Calvin notes the same ambiguity and reports Marckius finding no reason for the proposed alteration of the Hebrew tense, the earlier verse describing a more complete and not an obscurer view.

Where the second station was they locate from the name. Gill says the field of Zophim is named from the watch tower and its watchmen, and reports Jarchi that it was a high place where a watchman stood to observe whether an army came against a city. Ellicott renders it the field of watchers and identifies it with the height from which Moses afterwards surveyed the promised land, described as the mountain of Nebo, allowing that Pisgah may have had more than one summit. Gill and Keil record the repetition without comment, Gill that Balak stood by his burnt offering as before and the Lord put a word in Balaam's mouth as before, Keil that Balaam went to meet the Lord yonder and returned with what he was given.

What Balak's question betrays Calvin takes hardest: he inquires what God had answered although he had rejected the previous revelation, and thus do hypocrites profess anxious solicitude in inquiring the will of God while the knowledge of it is intolerable to them. Clarke reads the question as a concession: Balak now understood that Balaam was wholly under Jehovah's influence and would say nothing but what God commanded, though, not knowing Jehovah as Balaam did, he still hoped God might change his mind. Ellicott notes only that Balak speaks of God under the name Jehovah. Henry turns the manoeuvre into two applications: see how restless the church's enemies are in their attempts to ruin it, leaving no stone unturned and no project untried, and would that we were as full of contrivance in good designs for the glory of God, or as earnest to obtain the blessing as Balak was to procure a curse, designedly upon Israel but really upon himself.
18:
The summons opening the second parable they read as rhetoric. Calvin says the expression means to use glowing and elevated language the more to awaken attention, and that the preface, calling on Balak to rise and hearken, has the same object. Wesley says the word implies the diligent attention required, that Balak rouse himself and carefully mind what is said.

That God does not lie or repent they gloss three ways. Gill argues from what God is: man consists of flesh and blood and a created finite soul, whereas God, though human parts are ascribed to him figuratively, is not to be conceived corporeally, much less as sinful man, who goes astray from the womb speaking lies. Clarke reads the line as a correction of Balak, who had supposed God could change his mind, and observes that even the heathen would not allow their supreme god to be caught in a falsity, citing Aeschylus. Ellicott turns it into evidence of another kind: Samuel's adoption of these words with slight variation shows his familiarity with this portion of the Pentateuch. Wesley defines both verbs, that to lie would be to break his promises and to repent to change his counsels, and adds the condition, unless he see iniquity in Jacob.

Why Balaam cannot revoke what he said Calvin makes a matter of constraint: a command to bless had been given and a positive law laid down, since he was not free in this matter but bound by God to the prophetic office even against his own will, so that it is not in his power to alter it. Keil puts the same in narrative terms, that Balaam meets Balak's expectation of a retraction with the declaration that he cannot turn the blessing; Gill, that he had commandment to bless Israel and declare them a happy people.

That God beheld no iniquity in Jacob is the hardest saying here, and they divide over it four ways. Gill takes it of non-imputation: not that there was no sin nor any observed, but that he did not mark it in strict justice to punish for it, forgiving it and hiding his face. Wesley narrows the term instead: the iniquity meant is not such as was in the Canaanites, which God punishes with utter destruction. Clarke calls the passage difficult and offers two escapes: if spoken of the people, whose iniquity was almost unparalleled, the saying cannot be strictly true, but if spoken of the patriarch Jacob, or of Jacob after he became Israel, it is strictly true, since a nobler character, Abraham excepted, is not to be found in history, and for his sake God is represented as sparing a rebellious people; alternatively the two Hebrew words may bear their commoner senses of trouble and afflictive labour, so that the promise is of protection rather than a verdict on character. Calvin rejects one answer by name. Some understand the words of idols, as though Israel were untainted by such offences, which he asks how any can say when they had so openly fallen into idolatry; the better sense is that no such iniquity is seen in Jacob as would rank him with the nations given to violence, though the difficulty returns, since the Israelites were scarcely better than the worst of mankind. Some reply feebly, he says, that it was not seen because God did not impute it; in his own opinion nothing else is meant than that the people pleased God because he had sanctified them, so that what is declared is not what they were but the grace which exalted them as a holy nation, as Jerusalem was the holy city while it was a den of thieves and Abraham's children are called holy branches from a holy root. Ellicott notes only that the same pair of words occurs in Habakkuk, and that shout renders the word used of the trumpet blast.
22:
The bringing out of Egypt they take as an argument from continuance. Ellicott renders it literally, that God is bringing them out, the participle denoting continuance, so that he who brought them forth was still conducting them; and he finds an allusion to Balak's words. Keil says the same of the grammar, that the participle is not a preterite but designates the leading. Calvin makes it a reason for their constant success: God, having once redeemed this people, will not forsake the work he has begun, the argument being drawn from the continued course of his blessings, which flow from an inexhaustible fountain. Gill puts it plainly, that he who brought them thence will not suffer them to perish; Wesley, that it was by a strong hand and in spite of all their enemies, the change from plural to singular being common in Hebrew.

What beast the horned creature is Clarke settles at length, against the English word. It is generally allowed that there is no such beast as the unicorn, a creature of the horse kind with one long curled horn, the creature painted from fancy being a supporter of the royal arms of Great Britain; That no single-horned animal can be intended is evident from Moses himself, who says of Joseph that he has the horns of a reem, plural horns with a singular animal; the creature is either the rhinoceros, some varieties of which have two horns, or the wild bull, and the rhinoceros seems to him likeliest. Keil renders the same word buffalo without argument.

The denial of enchantment Calvin sets out as three competing readings before choosing. It is commonly expounded as an encomium on the people, as not given to enchantments and magical superstitions, which the law forbade; others, that the Israelites shall not want enchanters, since by Urim or by the prophets God would reveal whatever was profitable; but their opinion is more correct who interpret it that no enchantment avails against the Israelites. In his own judgment Balaam confesses that there is no room for his enchantments, his arts failing him, a confession which harmonizes with the words of Pharaoh's magicians, this is the finger of God. Clarke and Gill take the third: Clarke, that because God has determined to save them no enchantment can prevail; Gill, that Balaam owns his enchantments signified nothing. Ellicott takes the first: rendering it that there is no augury in Jacob and no divination in Israel, he says they had no need of augury, since God revealed to them his acts and his will, and quotes Hengstenberg that this applies to the Church of all ages, the wisdom of this world resembling augury while the Church knows from God's Word what God does.

What the closing figure grants they carefully limit. Ellicott and Gill both prefer the lioness, Gill reporting from Aelian that she is the strongest and most warlike beast, and Ellicott noting that Balaam transfers to the whole nation what Jacob prophesied of Judah alone. Clarke keeps the lion, the great or old one, king of the forest, feared by all the beasts of the field, so that Israel shall be the subduer and possessor of Canaan. Wesley reads the image of action, that as a lion rouses itself to the prey, so shall Israel stir itself against its enemies and not rest from pursuing. Calvin enters the one caution: the comparison is not in every respect accurate, since it does not make the Israelites cruel or rapacious, but merely bold and strong and prompt in resistance if any provoke them. On the clause about what God has wrought Clarke would read that as at this time it shall be told what God works, Ellicott that at the set time it is told to Jacob what God has done, and Wesley exclaims at works which will be matter of admiration to all ages.
25:
What Balak means by neither curse nor bless Gill and Keil read as exasperation rather than instruction. Gill says it signifies that it would be as well or better to do nothing at all than to do what he did, and that the sense is not that Balak would not have him curse them, since that was the one thing he wanted, but that he could not bear the blessing. Keil says Balak was not deterred and at first exclaimed in indignation. Calvin makes the outburst a specimen of a general condition: here we may behold as in a mirror how wretchedly unbelievers are driven to and fro, alternating between vain hopes and fears, and how their changes of purpose bring them back again to the same errors.

What Balaam's answer confesses Calvin takes as the whole of his position. The mercenary prophet here confesses that he has no more power of himself to be silent than to speak; nor is there any doubt that he would excuse himself with servility to the proud king, to whom he would willingly have sold himself. Gill hears the same words as a claim to character, that Balaam appeals to Balak for his honesty and faithfulness, being one who would be thought honest and faithful both to God and man, since he had told him plainly at their first meeting what he must expect. Keil records the answer as the narrative gives it, that all the Lord speaks, that he must do.

Why Balak tried a third station Gill explains on a different principle from the second attempt. The new place was proposed not because it was better for a view of the people but because it was a more religious place, on which account the king hoped for success. Ellicott marks a change in Balak's own language, that he here makes mention of God under the name Elohim, and that he appears satisfied that Balaam was hindered by God from uttering the curses he wished pronounced. Gill adds why Balaam consented, that he was willing to try again and to gratify the king, and especially to get the wages of unrighteousness, which he dearly loved, as the apostle says.

Where the third station was they place and characterise together. Gill says Peor was a high mountain in Moab, so called from a gap or opening in it, where the idol Baal was worshipped and whence he had the name Baal-peor, and where very probably there was a temple. Clarke says the same and adds the character of the worship, that this was probably the place where the famous Baal-peor had his chief temple, and that he appears to have been the Priapus of the Moabites, worshipped with the same obscene and abominable rites. Wesley calls it a high place named Beth-peor, the house or temple of Peor, so called because Baal-peor was worshipped there. Ellicott gives the topography instead, that Mount Peor was one peak of the northern part of the mountains of Abarim, nearer than the other heights to the camp of the Israelites, and that it looked toward or over the face of Jeshimon, that is, the waste or desert. On the rites that followed Keil notes only that the sacrifices offered in preparation for this fresh attempt were the same as in the former cases, and Gill that although they were expensive Balak did not grudge them but spared no cost to gain his point, though he could now have but little hope of it.
